CRITERIA:
Each Brownfield Advisory Committee shall consist of an odd number of members numbering no less than three and no more than seven, each of whom shall be appointed by the City Commission to serve for the duration of the Committee, unless a different term shall be set by the City Commission. The City Commission may appoint or remove members of the Committee at any time. The members may or may not be City residents, but should have a relation to the area in which the Committee has jurisdiction such as a resident, business owner, property owner, and the City Commission should strive to appoint one or more members with training or expertise in the fields of environmental science and economic development. The City Manager or his designee shall serve as an ex officio member of the Committee who shall not have a vote, but may be elected to be a presiding officer and shall serve as a City Commission liaison to the Committee.
DUTIES:
The Brownfield Advisory Committee shall:
(1). Be responsible for making recommendations to the City Commission regarding brownfields within the City.
(2). Receive public comment on the rehabilitation and redevelopment of brownfields areas, future land use, local employment opportunities, community safety and economic justice. The Committee will also review outreach efforts and materials.
(3). Review and recommend ways to encourage public interest and participation in the brownfields initiatives of the City.
(4). Invite persons to its meetings in an effort to provide local knowledge concerning the location of potentially contaminated sites and the possibility of redevelopment.
(5). Provide periodic reports to the City Commission either when directed to do so by the City Commission or the City Manager or on its own accord.

description:
This request is for approval to annex ±20.13 acres of property into the City of DeLand to develop a residential project with a subsequent land use amendment to Medium Density Residential and a rezone request to the DeLand Reserve Planned Development.
The City’s guidelines for annexation require a property to be sufficiently contiguous to property already within the city limits and accessible to public services provided. In addition, the State requires the property be reasonably compact, not circuitous, and does not create an enclave. The subject property is contiguous to the City of DeLand, is reasonably compact, is not circuitous and will not create an enclave.
At their September 10, 2025, meeting, the Planning Board recommended approval of the annexation. On October 6, 2025, City Commission approved the annexation on first reading.

description:
The request is to amend the land use designation of the subject property from Volusia County Rural to City of DeLand Medium Density Residential (MDR), for ±20.13 acres of property. The subject property is also located within the City’s Transit Oriented Development/ Redevelopment area, and the future land use is Medium-Density Residential. The 2050 Vision plan, describes the Transit Oriented Development/Redevelopment area as being an area that will encourage higher density and a mixture of uses, in order to make a transit system more efficient for the DeLand area. These areas will see a transition from the current development pattern to a more transit-friendly pattern, over time.
The Comprehensive Plan describes the Medium-Density Residential land use designation as being typified by detached and attached moderate density housing types, serving as a transitional area between nonresidential or high-density residential and low-density residential land use with a maximum density of 12 dwelling units per acre. The development should provide recreation and open space through the clustering of dwelling units and shall include on-site amenities such as, but not limited to, recreational facilities, open space, and pedestrian walkways.
The proposed maximum density of 8 dwelling units per acre provides a transition from the lower density residential to the higher density residential and proposed nonresidential/residential uses within this area, specifically on the southern side of SR-44. The subject property is ±1.6 miles from the DeLand SunRail station, and the applicant has coordinated with Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) and Volusia County to provide a more transit-friendly pattern by constructing additional sidewalks along North Ridgewood Avenue and State Road 44. Therefore, the request is compatible with the Comprehensive Plan and the 2050 Vision Plan.
On-site community enhancements are being provided in the DeLand Reserve PD including:
Walking paths, one centrally located and one within the Tree Protection Area (TPA), adhering to the TPA requirements in the Land Development Regulations.
Internal sidewalks that connect the entire site to the new proposed sidewalk along N. Ridgewood Ave.
A dog park
A tot lot
Open space throughout the site
Centrally located community gathering area
The proposed land use designation, Medium-Density Residential, is consistent with the surrounding area, and is not expected to create any land use incompatibilities.
At the September 10, 2025, meeting, the Planning Board recommended approval of the land use amendment.
On October 6, 2025, City Commission approved the small scale land use amendment on first reading.
On November 5, 2025, the Volusia Growth Management Commission (VGMC) issued a certificate of consistency.
title: Second Reading of Ordinance No. 2025-20, Changing the Land Use for ±20.13 Acres of Property, Located at 210 North Ridgewood Avenue, from Volusia County Rural to City of DeLand Medium-Density Residential (MDR). First Reading held on October 6, 2025.

description:
The applicant is requesting to rezone the subject property from Volusia County A-3C (Transitional Agriculture with a Thoroughfare Overlay Zone overlay), to the DeLand Reserve PD (Planned Development) district. The DeLand Reserve PD, is a residential planned development and includes the western 25-ft right-of-way of North Ridgewood Avenue, as it was never dedicated to Volusia County. At the time of the subdivision process, the applicant will dedicate the necessary 25-ft right-of-way as well as additional right-of-way to Volusia County for a sidewalk along North Ridgewood.
The proposed Planned Development rezoning will allow for the applicant to develop the site into a 155-unit maximum residential subdivision. Included in the PD are standards to allow for the flexibility of all single-family, all multi-family units or a mixture of each. The standards also allow for the flexibility of a mixture of front loaded, rear loaded, and zero-lot line single-family units. However, the applicant is only proposing a mixture of front loaded and rear loaded multi-family units at this time.
The conceptual plan shows two access points from N. Ridgewood Avenue, minimum of 40% of open space, which shall include the minimum 15% of Tree Protection Area, that will serve as a buffer between the existing neighborhood to the north and the commercial/industrial use to the west. Additionally, the development includes two connected meaningful, accessible open space areas, with meandering paths, one in the northwest corner and one in the middle of the development, which creates a pedestrian corridor that is beneficial for the community.
The proposed development includes a minimum of 20’ wide lots for townhomes and 30’ wide lots for single-family. Parking shall be provided at a ratio of two (2) parking spaces per residential lot, together with an additional allocation of 0.25 guest parking spaces per residential lot, accommodated by on-street parking spaces provided throughout the development for visitors. The subject property is located ±1.6 miles from the DeLand Sunrail station, therefore, the applicant has designed a more transit friendly pattern by proposing internal sidewalks, and an additional sidewalk along North Ridgewood Avenue connecting to the existing sidewalk network and anticipated future developments in the area.
The development includes landscape designs that will serve environmentally friendly functions including, but not limited to, cooling, privacy screening, shade, aesthetics, wildlife habitat, runoff pollution prevention. The design shall incorporate green infrastructure such as stormwater plantings, rain gardens and/or vegetative swales as appropriate to mimic the natural environment.

description:
The applicant has been working with the County since 2021 seeking approval to construct a subdivision with a combination of single-family homes and townhomes. The project was initially put on hold because of a conflict between the minimum density requirements of the County’s Comprehensive Plan and the dimensional requirements for single-family residences in the Southwest Activity Center zoning designation. The Southwest Activity Center was originally visioned as a major employment and commerce center near the I-4 interchange with a variety of housing choices to support the employment base. To spur economic development, and to resolve the conflicts between the Comprehensive Plan and the Zoning, County staff proposed modifications to the SWR and SWC zoning designations, which were approved in 2023. The applicant then proceeded with plat and construction plan review for the subdivision.
The City and the County of Volusia have a long-standing utility service agreement (USA) which regulates the provision of utilities by the City outside the corporate limits of the City. In November 2022, the City and the County concluded a years-long negotiation process to amend the USA to include additional areas outside City limits that would be served by City utilities. One of the areas added included the subject property.
If this project had been in the City’s utility service area when it started the development review process, the developer would have been required to obtain utilities from the City and because of its contiguity to the city limits, would have been required to annex and then go through a land use and zoning change prior to undertaking development review. However, since the developer was already fairly far along in the development review and entitlement process, the developer was entitled to proceed with development in the County and under County regulations.
To avoid further project delays, the applicant continued with plat approval, while concurrently submitting applications for incorporation into the City. The application for annexation is accompanied by a request for a small-scale future land use map amendment (SMLU25-025) and a request for a Planned Development (PD) rezone (Z25-024).
The City could simply annex the property and not change the future land use and zoning designations for the property, in which case the property would retain its county land use and zoning designations and would subject to the County’s subdivision regulations pursuant to Section 171.062(2), Florida Statutes.
City staff believes that it is much better to change the land use and zoning designations to City designations as it will be much more conducive to the City’s ongoing regulation of the development.
During the review of those applications, the applicant received County approval to begin site and infrastructure work to service the development. That construction activity is currently ongoing. The property was partially wooded and undeveloped. It did not appear to contain any wetlands and does not lie within the 100-year flood zone.
If the requests are approved, the County will continue to monitor and inspect all site improvements required by the development order. Prior to any vertical construction, the City will inspect access and utilities for life safety. A site plan will be required for the community amenity center. Building permits for the individual lots will be administered through the City. The City has received several complaints from nearby residents regarding construction activity. The City is currently coordinating with both the County and applicant to resolve resident concerns.
At the September 10, 2025 Planning Board meeting, the Board voted unanimously (5-0) to recommend approval of the request for annexation.
On October 6, 2025, the City Commission approved the annexation on first reading.

description:
The subject property is located directly south of the West Volusia Shopping Center, across from Firehouse Rd. It was previously rezoned from C-2, General Commercial, to the Mainstreet Townhomes Planned Development (PD) on August 7, 2006. The Mainstreet Townhomes PD approved 66 multi-family townhome units, but the project was abandoned after the rezoning was approved.
The C-2 zoning district allows for a range of commercial uses such as office/medical uses, personal service uses, hospitality uses as well as vehicular service uses and multi-family uses. The C-2 zoned district differs from the Mainstreet Townhomes PD which only allows multi-family townhomes as a permitted use.
On June 11, 2025, the Planning Board voted 3-1 to recommend denial of the rezone request. At the meeting, both citizens and Board members voiced concern over the uncertainty of future development and impacts upon the neighboring Wellington Woods residential subdivision located directly to the east of the subject property.
On July 21, 2025, the City Commission voted to continue the request to the August 18, 2025, City Commission meeting.
On August 18, 2025, the City Commission voted to continue the request to the October 6, 2025, City Commission meeting.
On October 6, 2025, the City Commission voted to continue the request to the November 17, 2025, City Commission meeting, allowing the applicant more time to meet with nearby residents of Wellington Woods and their concerns.
On October 24, 2025, a neighborhood meeting was held and attended by the applicant, Jessica Gow of CobbCole, the owners of the subject property and 8 adjacent residents from Wellington Woods. The topics discussed included:
Distance from Carwash building to rear property line (645 ft., about an 8th of a mile) and sound buffering, which should not be an issue with that distance.
Distance from the homeowners' property line to future potential development in the rear of the property – the discussion centered around the Property Owner and residents agreeing that the potential for retail development in that corridor was highly unlikely based on site layout, and the residents requested, and the owner agreed, that the owner will work with the City to install opaque fencing along that boundary when/if development in the rear moves forward – inside of the 25’ setback/natural preservation area proposed.
Residents agreed there is no need for a written use restriction based on the practical constraints of the site and limitations on uses in the rear.
Residents and Property Owner agreed that based on the info discussed, they would no longer oppose the zoning request with the assurance there would be a fence in the area discussed.One resident did continue to express frustration that they were told the subject property would be preservation area by the realtor.
The residents, headed up by Jim Peppin as their point of contact, noted that they would either send notes to the Commissioners noting that they were comfortable, or organize to have someone at the meeting to say they are satisfied and not opposed to the rezoning.
title: First Reading of Ordinance Changing the Zoning for Approximately 7.35 Acres of Property, Located on South Woodland Boulevard from Mainstreet Townhomes PD to C-2 (General Commercial). First Reading Continued on October 6, 2025.

description:
The FY 2025-2026 Budget includes funds for a roof replacement for City Hall. The amount of funding that was included is approximately $331,000. The roof is at the end of its useful life, out of warranty, and has needed to incur regular patching and maintenance over the past 5 years. There also has been interior damage in certain instances due to the deterioration of the roof. These repairs cost the city money and include things like repeated ceiling tile replacement, dry wall/paint repairs, and carpet repairs/replacement.
The city has recently received a project proposal from a vendor through a cooperative purchasing program that is approximately $103,000 below the budgeted amount if we were to do a standard roof replacement that will include a 20-year warranty.
The vendor also quoted an alternative option to include solar panels on the roof that will offset 16.5% of the annual kWh consumed at City Hall, or stated differently, approximately $23,000 a year in energy savings. The solar system will have a similar warranty as compared to the roof on most components. The cost to add the solar option to the roof replacement would increase the total project to $462,198. According to the vendor, the payback period for adding the solar to the project would be just under 9 years. The city would see immediate savings on our monthly power bills. Additionally, an added benefit to utilizing a single vendor for this entire project is that if there are any issues, it is one touchpoint interaction. There will not be multiple touchpoints (or potential finger pointing) compared to if the city were to select a separate vendor for the solar separate from the roof vendor.
Staff is seeking direction from the City Commission as to how to proceed. The vendor needs to have a response by the end of November to lock in the pricing due to the Federal Solar Incentive Program changes that will be occurring at year end.
title: Consideration re Addition of Solar to the City Hall Roof Project.

description:
The City bid janitorial services last in 2020 and awarded the contract to High Sources Inc. to service various municipal facilities.
With the existing agreement out of extensions at the end of this calendar year, staff sought out proposals to ensure pricing was still competitive and service was on par with expectations. The Request for Proposal (RFP) was advertised locally and on the internet. The RFP focuses on separating basic janitorial services from the specialized optional services, which include hard floor care, carpet care and upholstery care. These specialized services are priced separately as an option to be performed on an as-needed basis rather than a scheduled basis.
A total of 19 proposals were received. The proposals were ranked by a Janitorial Review Committee that compared the proposals by price, experience/qualifications, and project approach. Then, the top four ranked proposals provided a follow-up presentation to the Committee for a final decision. After careful consideration, the Janitorial Review Committee ranked Southern Cleaning Services, Inc. as the top vendor.
Included with this RCA is the initial RFP, final ranking sheet and the completed RFP by Southern Cleaning Services, Inc.
title: Consideration re Award of Contract to Southern Cleaning Service, Inc. for Janitorial Services.

description:
DeLand Animal Services picks up stray dogs, sick or injured cats, and abandoned kittens within the City limits. We hold stray and abandoned dogs at the Second Chance Facility for (3) days allowing the opportunity for the owner to be reunited with their dog. We partner and communicate with area rescue groups in an attempt to place animals into a forever home. The dogs are then transported to Southeast Volusia Humane Society for shelter and adoption. Aggressive dogs and cats are immediately taken to Southeast Volusia Humane Society to be evaluated by their behavioral staff.
This agreement also allows City of DeLand residents to surrender their dogs and cats as well as drop off stray dogs or cats to Southeast Volusia Humane Society at the City's expense.
title: Consideration re Agreement for Services with Southeast Volusia Humane Society.

description:
The City of DeLand has been operating the Second Chance Facility since July of 2009. The facility temporarily houses cats and dogs that have been collected by the City’s animal control officers during the course of his/her duties. The facility allows the opportunity for the animals to be adopted through various rescue groups with which the City has partnered.
It is imperative that the City has a place to take animals in the instances when the Second Chance Facility is full, when the stray animals are not adopted, if the stray animals are considered aggressive, or ones that are in need of immediate medical care. In addition, the City permits residents to surrender domesticated animals to the shelter at the City's expense. Toward that end, the City desires to contract with West Volusia Humane Society, Inc. DBA New Hope Animal Shelter again this year. Contracting with New Hope Animal Shelter and Southeast Humane Society will provide the City with two no-kill shelter options in the event our shelter reaches full capacity.
title: Consideration re Agreement for Services with New Hope Animal Shelter.

description:
LDM Rentals LLC is requesting approval to remove one historic tree located at 134 North High Street. The Land Development Regulations require that, before the removal of any historic trees should occur, it shall be approved by the City Commission. Section 33-57.05(d) states that there must be a finding that the tree is a hazard (due to health or natural damage) or that it is not economically or practically feasible to develop the parcel without removing the tree. The City Forester has determined that the tree proposed for removal is a 51” DBH historic Live Oak in poor condition. The applicant, LDM Rentals LLC, is requesting the removal because the tree is a hazard due to its poor condition.
At the October 14th Tree Advisory Committee meeting, the Arborist Inspector’s PowerPoint was presented demonstrating the tree proposed for removal is a 51” DBH historic Live Oak in poor structural condition with approximately 40% of the crown left. The applicant is requesting the removal of the tree because the tree is a hazard due to its poor structural condition. Staff recommended approval for the removal of the historic tree due to its poor condition with a 100 percent DBH inches replacement requirement to be accomplished via the planting of a minimum of two (2) six- (6-) inch caliper canopy trees on the property with the remaining inches that are not planted on site contributed into the Tree Replacement Reserve Account. The Tree Advisory Committee did not recommend approval of the removal of the 51” Live Oak tree by a 2-3 vote. It was the opinion of those members voting against the removal that preserving the tree would maintain canopy coverage.
title: Resolution Approving the Removal of One Historic Tree, Located at 134 North High Street.

description:
Volusia County has received CDBG-DR funds from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) for disaster recovery efforts following Hurricanes Ian and Milton. In June, staff applied for a grant to acquire a 2-unit townhouse and storm water expansion. description:
In 2023, the City Commission directed staff to research and explore how Tiny Home Communities could function within City limits as the City’s current Land Development Regulations (LDRs) do not provide for Tiny Home Communities. In 2024, staff presented findings to both the City Commission and Planning Board to gather feedback. Staff then outlined code revisions based on City Commission and Planning Board feedback. In August 2025, staff hosted an open house with the public and conducted an online survey to gather further input. Public feedback at the open house was overwhelmingly positive with an overall sentiment that tiny homes are an appropriate housing option. The survey confirmed this sentiment with 83 % of the 253 total responses in favor of allowing Tiny Home Communities.
As such, staff is recommending revisions to the Land Development Regulations related to Tiny Home Communities. The draft regulations and Design Book are attached to this Commission packet. The design book to be adopted by reference will include sample elevations and designs for stakeholders to utilize as inspiration for potential projects.
At the September 10, 2025, Planning Board meeting, the Board voted unanimously (5-0) to recommend adoption of the proposed regulations as presented. On October 6, 2025, the City Commission voted to approve First Reading of this Ordinance.
In conjunction with the code update, to allow for tiny homes to be permitted under the Florida Building Code, the City must adopt Appendix Q — Tiny Houses, which is part of the Florida Building Code.
title: Second Reading of Ordinance No.2025-16, Amending Land Development Regulations, Sections 33-17, 33-19.15, and 33-12, Regarding Tiny Home Communities.

title: Second Reading of Ordinance No.2025-17, Amending Section 7-2, “Local Supplements to the Florida Building Code, Administration,” Subsection 101.2.3(4), to Add Appendix Q.

description:
The subject property is located within the R-1 Single-Family residential zoning district and has a future land use designation of Medium Density Residential, and is located within the Historic Garden District. The property is owned by the applicant, Michael Arth and is currently developed with a single-family residence and accessory dwelling unit. The applicant is requesting a special exception approval to permit a bed and breakfast homestay on their property.
The surrounding area consists of single-family, multiple-family, and commercial uses. The property is also located within the Historic Garden District, which consists of numerous historic buildings southeast of downtown. The subject property is developed with a single-family residence, and an accessory dwelling unit, and also contains a parking area previously constructed for an off-site commercial use, which has since been abandoned. The applicant received approval for several variance requests to reduce setbacks and buffers to construct the existing buildings and is now seeking special exception approval to permit a bed and breakfast homestay. If approved, the applicant intends to operate a bed and breakfast homestay with (1) guestroom in the primary structure, and two (2) additional guestrooms in an accessory building.The R-1 zone district allows a bed and breakfast homestay by special exception subject to the requirements of Sec. 33-27.03. If the structure to be used for a bed and breakfast is not 50 years old or is proposed to be located within an accessory structure, special exception review is required. Prior to 2017, an applicant seeking to permit a bed and breakfast homestay would have been required to meet these standards without the option for relief through a special exception. In 2017, the City Commission adopted Ordinance 2017-24 to allow bed and breakfast homestays to be established in areas where they were previously not permitted through the special exception process subject to Sec. 33-134.
On September 10, 2025 the Planning Board voted to recommend approval to the City Commission, subject to the applicant obtaining variance approval to reduce the required landscape buffers.
On October 6, 2025 the City Commission voted to continue this item to the October 20 meeting in consideration of ​a variance application.
On October 9, 2025 the Planning Board granted variance relief from the code requirement to provide landscape buffers around a bed and breakfast homestay.
title: Resolution Approving a Special Exception for a Bed and Breakfast Homestay, Located at 302 South Hayden Avenue.

description:
The applicant is requesting to demolish a building built prior to 1950, constructed in 1915 per the Volusia County Property Appraiser. This building is located north (behind) the main structure on the property. This property is located within the Downtown Historic Support District and Historic Support District. At this time, the applicant has not stated if they have had the building inspected for structural integrity, nor have they provided information regarding repairing the building to save it from collapse. However, they have stated there are no definite plans to reuse the property and intend for the property to be used as informal green space. Therefore, an application for redevelopment has yet to be submitted for review and demolition of historic buildings without definitive plans for redevelopment is discouraged by the City's codes.
At the August 7, 2025, meeting, the City of DeLand Historic Preservation Board motioned to approve the demolition of a building built prior to 1950 located at 207 ½ East Michigan Avenue. The vote on the motion resulted in a tie (2-2) because we do not have a full complement of members on the HPB. As such, no recommendation was made by the HPB.
At the August 18, 2025, meeting, the City Commission denied the demolition request. The applicant appeared at the September 3, 2025 Commission meeting asking for reconsideration. The City Commission agreed to reconsider the demolition request.
title: Resolution Approving or Denying the Demolition of a Building Built Prior to 1950, Located at 207 1/2 East Michigan Avenue.

attachments.name: Staff Report  - 225 W. New York Ave Apartments
Staff Report - Parking Reduction Request April 21, 2025 Commission Staff Report

description:
The applicant is requesting approval of a Class IV site plan to construct a 6-story building for 84 affordable apartments, with an approved parking reduction for 94 on-site parking spaces and 20 off-site parking spaces. The 1.63-acre site is located at 225 W. New York Avenue, and consists of two (2) parcels, zoned C-2A and C-2A (with the Historic Overlay), and was once the site of the Historic Putnam Hotel. The property is located within the Historic Design District with a portion located within the Downtown Historic District. The Future Land Use Designation is Downtown Commercial. Due to the size of the project (>80 units), a Class IV site plan is required.
Since the site layout depended on the parking reduction, the applicant requested approval from the City Commission for the parking reduction, as well as approval to use off-site parking on County property, before bringing the request for site plan approval to City Commission. On April 21, 2025, the applicant proposed 94 off-street parking spaces, a 28-space increase over the initial parking reduction request. This increased parking could be accomplished by increasing the building height to allow for ground floor parking under a portion of the building, bringing the proposed building height to 77 feet. The City Commission conditionally approved the parking, provided 20 additional off-site parking spaces could be secured for the project.
On July 21, 2025, the City Commission approved the parking reduction request, as the applicant was able to secure 20 additional off-site parking spaces on the adjacent Volusia County parking lot.
Prior to submitting the site plan, the applicant requested review of a concept plan to gather preliminary feedback ahead of the submittal. The concept plan was reviewed by the Technical Advisory Committee (TRC) on March 21, 2024, Planning Board on April 10, 2024, and City Commission on May 3, 2024. The TRC provided comments related to the site plan submittal requirements and expressed concerns regarding the mass, scale, context, activation of the street frontage, lack of ground floor commercial, colors, materials, access, parking, and general site design. Planning Board provided comments regarding inadequate parking, building architecture, proposed colors and materials, and lack of amenities for the residents. The City Commission provided similar comments. The applicant revised the concept and submitted a Class IV site plan on June 26, 2024.
Due to the size of the site, an environmental report is not required. The site was previously developed and has remained vacant since the demolition of the former Putnam Hotel. The applicant has worked with the City’s Forester to minimize impact to the 25-inch Diameter at Breast Height (DBH) Live Oak historic tree on the adjacent property.
An underground stormwater system has been designed to retain on-site a 100-year, 24-hour storm event.
The proposed building shall comply with section 33-94 – Community Design Standards. Since this site is located in the Historic District and the Historic Design District, a Certificate of Appropriateness (COA) is required. The Historic Preservation Board (HPB) reviewed the revised architecture for the 6-story building on June 5, 2025 and approved a COA as presented.
Landscape buffers are not required along street frontages in the C-2A zoning district (33-92.02(b)1). Properties within the C-2A zoning district are also not subject to the buffer requirements (33-17.17) and the vehicle use separation area may be reduced to 0-feet (33-91.06(a)2). The project will incorporate Florida Friendly landscaping.
The Volusia County School District has issued a letter indicating that the proposed project would not exceed the adopted level of service at any school level and stated that there is no objection to the proposed site plan (letter dated August 19, 2024 is attached).
A shared access driveway off of W. New York Avenue, located on county-owned property on the project’s west boundary, is proposed to provide the only site access. It is recommended that a cross-access easement shall be recorded and the recordation information shall be included on the site plan prior to issuance of a development order. A Traffic Impact memo for this proposed 84-unit affordable housing project was completed on October 2, 2024. The analysis determined that the project will generate 453 average daily trips, 35 peak hour A.M. and 46 peak hour P.M. trips. Per Sec. 33-41.04 of the LDR, a full Traffic Impact Analysis is not required for projects that generate less than 1,000 daily trips. A copy of the traffic memo is attached.
After three (3) rounds of review by the Technical Review Committee, on May 15, 2025, the TRC recommended the item be forwarded to the Planning Board once all of the outstanding comments have been satisfied.
At the September 10, 2025, Planning Board meeting, the Board voted (4-1) to recommend approval of the request for a Class IV site plan with the following three conditions of approval:The site plan must be revised to include a reference to the 20 off-site parking spaces prior to scheduling this item for City Commission.
A cross-access easement agreement must be recorded for the site access on the adjacent Volusia County site and the recordation information shall be added to the site plan, prior to the issuance of a development order.
The off-site parking agreement must be approved by Volusia County and the recordation information shall be included on the site plan, prior to the issuance of a development order.
The applicant has revised the site plan to add a reference to the 20 off-site parking spaces and this revised site plan is attached to this agenda item.
title: Resolution Approving Class IV Site Plan, New York Ave Apartments, Located at 225 West New York Avenue.

description:
The subject property is located directly south of the West Volusia Shopping Center, across from Firehouse Rd. It was previously rezoned from C-2, General Commercial, to the Mainstreet Townhomes Planned Development (PD) on August 7, 2006. The Mainstreet Townhomes PD approved 66 multi-family townhome units, but the project was abandoned after the rezoning was approved.
The C-2 zoning district allows for a range of commercial uses such as office/medical uses, personal service uses, hospitality uses as well as vehicular service uses and multi-family uses. The C-2 zoned district differs from the Mainstreet Townhomes PD which only allows multi-family townhomes as a permitted use.

At the meeting, both citizens and Board members voiced concern over the uncertainty of future development and impacts upon the neighboring Wellington Woods residential subdivision located directly to the east of the subject property.
On July 21, 2025, the City Commission voted to continue the request to the August 18, 2025, City Commission meeting.
On August 18, 2025, the City Commission voted to continue the request to the October 6, 2025, City Commission meeting.

The City’s guidelines for annexation require a property to be sufficiently contiguous to property already within the city limits and accessible to public services provided. In addition, the State requires the property be reasonably compact, not circuitous, and does not create an enclave. The subject property is contiguous to the City of DeLand, is reasonably compact, is not circuitous and will not create an enclave.
At their September 10, 2025, meeting, the Planning Board recommended approval of the annexation.

description:
The request is to amend the land use designation of the subject property from Volusia County Rural to City of DeLand Medium Density Residential (MDR), for ±20.13 acres of property. The subject property is also located within the City’s Transit Oriented Development/ Redevelopment area, and the future land use is Medium-Density Residential. The 2050 Vision plan, describes the Transit Oriented Development/Redevelopment area as being an area that will encourage higher density and a mixture of uses, in order to make a transit system more efficient for the DeLand area. These areas will see a transition from the current development pattern to a more transit-friendly pattern, over time.
The Comprehensive Plan describes the Medium-Density Residential land use designation as being typified by detached and attached moderate density housing types, serving as a transitional area between nonresidential or high-density residential and low-density residential land use with a maximum density of 12 dwelling units per acre. The development should provide recreation and open space through the clustering of dwelling units and shall include on-site amenities such as, but not limited to, recreational facilities, open space, and pedestrian walkways.
The proposed maximum density of 8 dwelling units per acre provides a transition from the lower density residential to the higher density residential and proposed nonresidential/residential uses within this area, specifically on the southern side of SR-44. The subject property is ±1.6 miles from the DeLand SunRail station, and the applicant has coordinated with Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) and Volusia County to provide a more transit-friendly pattern by constructing additional sidewalks along North Ridgewood Avenue and State Road 44. Therefore, the request is compatible with the Comprehensive Plan and the 2050 Vision Plan.
Two on-site community enhancements are being provided in the DeLand Reserve PD. These enhancements include:
Walking paths, one centrally located and one within the Tree Protection Area (TPA), adhering to the TPA requirements in the Land Development Regulations.
Internal sidewalks that connect the entire site to the new proposed sidewalk along N. Ridgewood Ave.
A dog park
A tot lot
Open space throughout the site
Centrally located community gathering area
The proposed land use designation, Medium-Density Residential, is consistent with the surrounding area, and is not expected to create any land use incompatibilities.
At the September 10, 2025, meeting, the Planning Board recommended approval of the land use amendment.
title: First Reading of Ordinance Changing the Land Use for ±20.13 Acres of Property, Located at 210 N Ridgewood Avenue, from Volusia County Rural to City of DeLand Medium-Density Residential (MDR).

description:
The applicant is requesting to rezone the subject property from Volusia County A-3C (Transitional Agriculture with a Thoroughfare Overlay Zone overlay), to the DeLand Reserve PD (Planned Development) district. The DeLand Reserve PD, is a residential planned development and includes the western 25-ft right-of-way of North Ridgewood Avenue, as it was never dedicated to Volusia County. At the time of the subdivision process, the applicant will dedicate the necessary 25-ft right-of-way as well as additional right-of-way to Volusia County for a sidewalk along North Ridgewood.
The proposed Planned Development rezoning will allow for the applicant to develop the site into a 155-unit maximum residential subdivision. Included in the PD are standards to allow for the flexibility of all single-family, all multi-family units or a mixture of each. The standards also allow for the flexibility of a mixture of front loaded, rear loaded, and zero-lot line single-family units. However, the applicant is only proposing a mixture of front loaded and rear loaded multi-family units at this time.
The conceptual plan shows two access points from N. Ridgewood Avenue, minimum of 40% of open space, which shall include the minimum 15% of Tree Protection Area, that will serve as a buffer between the existing neighborhood to the north and the commercial/industrial use to the west. Additionally, the development includes two connected meaningful, accessible open space areas, with meandering paths, one in the northwest corner and one in the middle of the development, which creates a pedestrian corridor that is beneficial for the community.
The proposed development includes a minimum of 20’ wide lots for townhomes and 30’ wide lots for single-family. Parking shall be provided at a ratio of two (2) parking spaces per residential lot, together with an additional allocation of 0.25 guest parking spaces per residential lot, accommodated by on-street parking spaces provided throughout the development for visitors. The subject property is located ±1.6 miles from the DeLand Sunrail station, therefore, the applicant has designed a more transit friendly pattern by proposing internal sidewalks, and an additional sidewalk along North Ridgewood Avenue connecting to the existing sidewalk network and anticipated future developments in the area.
The development includes landscape designs that will serve environmentally friendly functions including, but not limited to, cooling, privacy screening, shade, aesthetics, wildlife habitat, runoff pollution prevention. The design shall incorporate green infrastructure such as stormwater plantings, rain gardens and/or vegetative swales as appropriate to mimic the natural environment.
The applicant has applied for annexation of property, as well as a land use amendment to create the overall residential development (AN25-082), (SMLU25-083) which are being reviewed concurrently with this zoning amendment.
On September 10, 2025, the Planning Board voted to recommend approval of the DeLand Reserve PD.
title: First Reading of Ordinance Changing the Zoning for ±20.13 Acres of Property, Located at 210 North Ridgewood Avenue, from Volusia County A-3C (Transitional Agricultural with Thoroughfare Overlay Zone) to DeLand Reserve PD (Planned Development).

description:
The applicant has been working with the County since 2021 seeking approval to construct a subdivision with a combination of single-family homes and townhomes. The project was initially put on hold because of a conflict between the minimum density requirements of the County’s Comprehensive Plan and the dimensional requirements for single-family residences in the Southwest Activity Center zoning designation. The Southwest Activity Center was originally visioned as a major employment and commerce center near the I-4 interchange with a variety of housing choices to support the employment base. To spur economic development, and to resolve the conflicts between the Comprehensive Plan and the Zoning, County staff proposed modifications to the SWR and SWC zoning designations, which were approved in 2023. The applicant then proceeded with plat and construction plan review for the subdivision.
The City and the County of Volusia have a long-standing utility service agreement (USA) which regulates the provision of utilities by the City outside the corporate limits of the City. In November 2022, the City and the County concluded a years-long negotiation process to amend the USA to include additional areas outside City limits that would be served by City utilities. One of the areas added included the subject property.
If this project had been in the City’s utility service area when it started the development review process, the developer would have been required to obtain utilities from the City and because of its contiguity to the city limits, would have been required to annex and then go through a land use and zoning change prior to undertaking development review. However, since the developer was already fairly far along in the development review and entitlement process, the developer was entitled to proceed with development in the County and under County regulations.
To avoid further project delays, the applicant continued with plat approval, while concurrently submitting applications for incorporation into the City. The application for annexation is accompanied by a request for a small-scale future land use map amendment (SMLU25-025) and a request for a Planned Development (PD) rezone (Z25-024).
The City could simply annex the property and not change the future land use and zoning designations for the property, in which case the property would retain its county land use and zoning designations and would subject to the County’s subdivision regulations pursuant to Section 171.062(2), Florida Statutes.
City staff believes that it is much better to change the land use and zoning designations to City designations as it will be much more conducive to the City’s ongoing regulation of the development.
During the review of those applications, the applicant received County approval to begin site and infrastructure work to service the development. That construction activity is currently ongoing. The property was partially wooded and undeveloped. It did not appear to contain any wetlands and does not lie within the 100-year flood zone.
If the requests are approved, the County will continue to monitor and inspect all site improvements required by the development order. Prior to any vertical construction, the City will inspect access and utilities for life safety. A site plan will be required for the community amenity center. Building permits for the individual lots will be administered through the City.
At the September 10, 2025 Planning Board meeting, the Board voted unanimously (5-0) to recommend approval of the request for annexation.

description:
The applicant, Sean Fortier of KCG, Inc., has submitted an application for the review and approval of a preliminary plat for the Taylor Ridge residential subdivision. The subject property has a zoning designation of PD (Taylor Ridge Planned Development) which was approved by the City Commission on February 5, 2024. The development is located at the northwest corner of Taylor Ave. and S. Blue Lake Ave. and is ±26.01 acres in size. The applicant seeks to develop the property into a 63-lot single-family residential subdivision.
The individual lots will be 60'x115' in size, with all lots meeting the dimensional requirements outlined in the Taylor Ridge PD agreement. Access will be provided from S. Blue Lake Ave. as well as from E. Taylor Rd. The development agreement states that the project will utilize low impact development measures to protect environmental features. The development includes enhanced amenities, as required by the TRD (Transitional Residential Development) land use designation from the City's Comprehensive Plan. The development provides internal sidewalks and bike lanes, enhanced recreational amenities and is located within a mile of an arterial roadway in accordance with the TRD requirements.
The project will have an overall density of approximately 2.4 units per acre. In general, unless otherwise stated in the PD Agreement, the development standards will mirror the R-1 district regulations from the city’s land development regulations. An amendment to the PD was unanimously approved by the City Commission on July 21, 2025, modifying the tree mitigation requirements for trees in poor health.
The proposed subdivision complies with the development standards set forth in Sec. 33-146 "Subdivision of Land" of the City's land development regulations as well as the standards in the development agreement "Taylor Ridge PD", also including the amended tree mitigation standards that were approved as part of the first amendment.
On May 29, 2024, the Volusia County School Board provided a School Concurrency Determination Letter with no objections from the Board.
A transportation analysis was done as part of the PD rezoning. However, one is not required, as the trips do not exceed the 1,000 average daily trip threshold.
Prior to issuance of a development order, all tree mitigation fees will be paid.
On August 14, 2024, the Planning Board recommended approval of the preliminary plat.
title: Resolution Approving the Preliminary Plat for Taylor Ridge, Located at the Northwest Corner of South Blue Lake Avenue and East Taylor Avenue.

description:
The 2018 Pierce (SE81) was initially brought to the Ten-8 service station for scheduled warranty repairs concerning body cracks. As Ten-8 is a certified Pierce dealer and service provider in Sanford, the opportunity was also taken to conduct a comprehensive review of several outstanding work orders. During this multipoint inspection, several issues were identified, including various oil leaks and a leaking engine air compressor. This led to the vehicle's transfer to a Cummins service provider. The Cummins provider, after reviewing the engine's symptoms and operating hours, recommended a midlife overhaul. This standard repair procedure includes a 3-year, 150,000-mile warranty and was estimated to cost a minimum of $46,546.53, with the final price subject to revision pending the discovery of additional issues during the overhaul. The ​final price came to $72,559.00.
In addition to the engine overhaul, several other issues were addressed:A damaged transmission cooler hose and clamp were replaced, and a transmission service was performed.
The pump panel step and ground lights were repaired.
The power steering system was serviced to correct black fluid.
A pump test was required and completed after the internal engine work.
Torn toe link boots on both sides were replaced.
The driveshaft's loose dust cover welds and failed u-joints, which were causing rattling and vibration, were repaired.
A kinked fuel vent hose was replaced, and the fuel neck's broken tack welds were repaired.
title: Consideration re Change Order with Ten-8 Fire Safety LLC. for Squad Engine 81 Engine Rebuild.

The cyber liability coverage remains the same from the previous year. The premium quoted is $20,208.00.

description:
The City of DeLand imposes impact fees on new development to help pay the proportional fair share of such development's demand for facilities. Impact fees are related to police, fire, general government and parks and recreation and are used to create additional service capacity for the impact created by growth. The City is entitled by law to impose such impact fees on development so long as the fees bear a proportionate relationship to the costs related to the demand on each category of service created by such development. Impact fees are a one time payment for new development to pay for its pro-rata share of the cost for new capital facilities/projects required to serve that development.
In particular, the City has experienced extraordinary increases in demand for and the cost of delivering new infrastructure to support the growth in population, resulting from factors including the need to build completely new facilities in new locations (as opposed to simply expanding existing facilities) due not only to population growth (the population grew by more than 22% since the last impact fee update) but also to the geographic expansion of the population centers and extraordinary increases in land and construction costs since 2019, when the fees were last updated.
Below is a summary of the update to the impact fees with their related categories:
Single Family
Multi-Family

Office
Industrial/Warehousing
Public/Institutional
Assisted Living Facilities

description:
Approximately 43 residents currently live at the DeLand Municipal Mobile Home Park. The current residents pay $300 per month for rent, regardless of the trailer size. The rent figure includes lot rental, property tax, lawn maintenance, water, sewer, garbage and stormwater. The City increased the monthly rental rates by $25 effective January 1, each of the last six years. Before that, the municipal mobile home park had not seen a rental increase since 2009. Similar parks in Volusia County range from an average of $567 per month for all age parks (so-called "family parks") to $827 per month for 55+ parks for lot rental alone. Due to this fact, staff recommends increasing the rental rate by another $25 per month. The proposed new lot rental rate would be $325 per month, regardless of the trailer size.
The lot rental increase requires a 90-day notice to the homeowners before it can take effect. Therefore, with approval from the City Commission, staff will send out notices during the month of September 2025 in order for the lot rental increases to take effect January 1, 2026.
title: Consideration re Rental Increases for DeLand Municipal Mobile Home Park.

Staff is proposing a number of changes to the program to encourage greater utilization of the funds to maintain strong and vibrant corridors. description:
The subject property is located directly south of the West Volusia Shopping Center, across from Firehouse Rd. It was previously rezoned from C-2, General Commercial, to the Mainstreet Townhomes Planned Development (PD) on August 7, 2006. The Mainstreet Townhomes PD approved 66 multi-family townhome units, but the project was abandoned after the rezoning was approved.
The C-2 zoning district allows for a range of commercial uses such as office/medical uses, personal service uses, hospitality uses as well as vehicular service uses and multi-family uses. The C-2 zoned district differs from the Mainstreet Townhomes PD which only allows multi-family townhomes as a permitted use.
On June 11, 2025, the Planning Board voted 3-1 to recommend denial of the rezone request. At the meeting, both citizens and Board members voiced concern over the uncertainty of future development and impacts upon the neighboring Wellington Woods residential subdivision located directly to the east of the subject property.
On July 21, 2025, the City Commission voted to continue the request to the August 18, 2025, City Commission meeting.
This is a request for continuance to the October 6, 2025, City Commission meeting.

description:
The City of DeLand is required to test and repair backflow devices throughout its Utility Service area. Presently, approximately 9,000 customers have city-maintained backflow devices that require annual testing. A small percentage of these devices (estimated to be approximately 200) are expected to fail the test annually and will need to be repaired or replaced.
In early 2020, the city bid for necessary backflow testing services. Pursuant to staff recommendations, the City Commission awarded the contract to Aaron’s Backflow Services Inc. The contract provided for a 2-year term with subsequent three 1-year renewals. During the term of this contract to date, this firm has performed in an acceptable manner. The decision to advertise in 2025 was based on the fact that no more remaining renewals were available with the current provider.
The project was advertised for bid via the local newspaper and the internet-based Demand Star System. Bids were received from only one firm and the results are presented in the attached bid tabulation. Due to the large numbers of sizes and types of devices that are to be tested, requested discounts for parts supplied and hourly rates for various items, the bid tabulation was further analyzed as depicted on the attached spreadsheet. The proposed contractor is the current vendor at this time and thus will allow a seamless transition to the new contract.
title: Consideration re Award of Bid for Backflow Device Testing, Certifications and Repairs for the City of DeLand FY 25-26.

description:
The applicant, Mark Watts of CobbCole, is seeking to vacate a portion of the Church Street right-of-way, lying north of lots 1-7 of the Delmay Subdivision. The vacation of the right-of-way will allow additional area for future development. The right-of-way being abandoned is 350' in length and 25' in width. Based on staff research, the north 25-feet of Church Street was not dedicated, as the Wesleyan Church property was part of the original City of DeLand corporate boundary plat. The property to the south is part of the Delmay Subdivision, and at the time of subdivision, 25-feet of rigth-of-way was dedicated. Lots 1-7 and a portion of Lots 22-24 of the Delmay Subdivision were reconfigured into three parcels.
At the April 7, 2025 hearing for first reading, the pastor raised concerns regarding the existing food pantry operations that take place along the southern portion of the church property, adjacent to the proposed townhome development. His concerns included the potential impact on the new residential development, such as the vehicle queuing, noise, and foot traffic associated with the weekly food pantry operations.The pastor was hopeful that the adjacent 25-feet of Church Street would be cleared for the benefit of the church and food pantry visitors. However, as previously mentioned, the northern portion of the Church Street right-of-way was never platted.
At the April 17, 2025, Technical Review Committee, Mr. Watts stated that he recently met with the pastor of the Wesleyan Church to discuss the pastor's concerns. They both agreed upon the installation of a 6' tall wall on the north side of the townhome development to buffer the activities between the two properies. As previously mentioned, the pastor also had concerns that the future townhome residents may take issue with some of the church operations, which could cause complaints. To mitigate this potential issue, Mr. Watts stated that he will be adding a disclosure to both the PD agreement and the covenants, that advises the future townhome residents that there is an active church behind their property to the north, and the church will be carrying on their general operations and various church-related activities. The pastor was satisfied with the disclosure being added to the two documents.
Staff has not received any other comments from the mailed notice, and the following utility providers provided letters of no-objection:
AT&T
Charter Communications
City of DeLand
Duke Energy
FL Gas Transmission Co.
Florida Public Utilities
On March 17, 2025, the City Commission voted to continue the abandonment of Church Street until the April 7, 2025, City Commission meeting.
On April 7, 2025, the City Commission voted unanimously to approve the abandonment on First Reading.
On April 21, 2025, the City Commission voted to continue the request to the May 5, 2025, City Commission meeting.
title: Second Reading of Ordinance No. 2025-06, Abandoning 0.198 Acres of Right-of-Way of Church Street, North of Lots 1-7 of the Delmay Subdivision Plat.

description:
Spurred by the recent attack in New Orleans and other areas, city staff began reexamining special event safety measures to ensure the safety of event goers. One of the most pressing issues noted was the risk of vehicles being used as weapons to attack attendees of large public events.
Current traffic control measures, such as traditional barricades, jersey barriers and heavy equipment/trucks that risk vehicle damage, are either insufficient, labor-intensive or impractical for rapid deployment.
To this end, staff is recommending the purchase of two additional items that would enhance the safety of downtown event attendees. Two items have been proposed: Meridian Barriers and traditional bollards. This agenda item is in regard to the purchase of Meridian Barriers that can be rapidly deployed during events. Meridian Barriers are deployed and look somewhat similar to Type III Barricades used at our events. However, the difference from the traditional Type III barricade is that the Meridian Barrier can stop a vehicle from entering an area using technology and physics. in short, the Type III Barricade is only a visual deterrent, not a physical and visual deterrent like the Meridian Barrier.
To this end, staff is recommending the purchase of 5 trailer sets (40 barriers total) of the Meridian Rapid Defense barrier system to be deployed at all major events throughout the city.
title: Consideration re Request to Purchase Meridian Rapid Defense Barrier System.

description:
Spurred by the recent attack in New Orleans and other areas, city staff began reexamining special event safety measures to ensure the safety of event goers. One of the most pressing issues noted was the risk of vehicles being used as weapons to attack attendees of large public events.
Current traffic control measures, such as traditional barricades, jersey barriers and heavy equipment/trucks that risk vehicle damage, are either insufficient, labor-intensive or impractical for rapid deployment, especially on frequent occasions.
To this end, staff is recommending the purchase of two additional items that would enhance the safety of downtown event attendees. Two items have been proposed: Meridian Barriers and traditional bollards. This agenda item is in regard to the purchase of additional bollards on our most popular event road: East & West Indiana Avenue, along with repositioning of the bollards on West Georgia Avenue to increase the protected area to allow for larger events. Bollards are a more traditional means to enhance event attendee safety at events. Bollards are physical structures that are placed in fixed locations. Bollards would be ideal for areas that have a high frequency of closures that are similar in nature. The Meridian Barriers, conversely, can be deployed anywhere but require a special trailer and jack system. Meridian Barriers are more costly to obtain and require more storage space when not in use.
Unlike the Meridian Barriers, which are able to be procured through state contract, the bollards will need to be procured through the city's bid process. The City's grant coordinator has noted that this item could be submitted in the summer for a potential grant opportunity, but the grant is a competitive grant, so the award opportunity is uncertain.
title: Consideration re Request to Purchase Additional Bollards for East and West Indiana Avenue Along with the Repositioning of Bollards on West Georgia Avenue.

description:

description:
The current Land Development Regulations (LDR) include community design standards (33-94) which apply to commercial, industrial, and multi-family residential projects throughout the City. These requirements provide standards for architectural elevations and site design. The current standards require the oversight of an architect; allow for an exception for chain link fencing if wire-coated and landscaped; and discourage monotonous repetition of structures, but without providing standards or criteria. Staff is proposing several updates to Section 33-94 to include criteria and a prohibition against the monotonous repetition of structures within a development or project area, Section 33-94.03(a)5.; to revise the requirement for oversight by an architect from “will” to “may”, Section 33-94.06(a)5.; to include detailed and dimensioned architectural elevations to demonstrate consistency with the community design standards and criteria, Section 33-94.02(c)2.; to remove the exception for landscaped, vinyl coated chain link fencing, Section 33-94.03 (h)4.; and to add a provision to exclude governmentally-owned properties within the Historic Design District and the Downtown Design District from Historic Preservation Board review, while still requiring governmentally-owned properties to meet the design criteria within 33-94.04(b).
On February 13, 2025, the Planning Board recommended approval of the proposed amendments, with a vote of 6-0.
On March 3, 2025, the City Commission approved the proposed revisions on first reading.
title: Second Reading of an Ordinance No. 2025-03, Amending Portions of Section 33-94 of the City of DeLand Land Development Regulations.

description:
Section 31 of the City Charter requires the City Commission to designate a firm of certified public accountants to perform an independent audit of the City's financial records. The City Commission renewed a contract with James Moore & Co., P.L. to audit its financial statements for a term of five years and the fiscal year ending September 30, 2024 is the first year of the renewed contract.
The audit of the financial records for the fiscal year 2023-2024 is complete and staff has prepared the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) presented herein. The ACFR provides a complete set of financial statements that are prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) that represent the financial position of the City and results of operations as of September 30, 2024. The City has received an unmodified audit opinion, which is the highest level of opinion the auditor can give and is, therefore, the opinion we seek to obtain each year.
The ACFR provides for an overview and narrative of financial activity and trends along with detailed and consolidated financial statements for all City funds. GAAP requires that management provide a narrative introduction, overview, and analysis to accompany the basic financial statements in the form of Management's Discussion and Analysis (MD&A). The City MD&A can be found immediately following the independent auditor's report.
title: Presentation of the Annual Comprehensive Audit Report (ACFR) for Fiscal Year Ended September 30, 2024.

description:
The FACC Board of Directors is considering how to pursue state legislation to provide a public records exemption for the personal information of current Municipal Clerks and employees who perform municipal elections work.
The City Commission of the City of Sanford, Florida, recently adopted a resolution urging the Florida State Legislature to enact legislation to provide a public records exemption for Municipal Clerks and employees who perform municipal elections work or have any part in code enforcement functions of a city and providing for an effective date.
Many municipal staff who perform duties that include, or result in, investigations into complaints regarding election fraud, legal enforcement of hearings related to neglect or abuse, or other activities that could lead to a criminal prosecution are exposed to threats and other acts of violence.
Municipal Clerks often administer elections. Some election workers have been targeted for threats and violence due to the nature of materials they are responsible for. Further, Clerks are often involved in legal enforcement proceedings in actions related to violations of codes and ordinances. Occasionally, these proceedings have led to retaliation and threats by defendants.
Please note, there are currently 27 public record exemptions for specific roles, one of which applies to Code Enforcement Officers. Code Officers are covered by the exemption, but not Municipal Clerks. There is language referencing code enforcement work in the resolution template for the purpose of including Municipal Clerks and employees who perform work related to code enforcement proceedings to be included as part of the public record exemption.
The Florida Association of City Clerks is asking The City of DeLand to adopt the resolution in support of the exemption.
title: Resolution Approving the Support of Public Records Exemption for Municipal Clerks and Employees who Perform Municipal Elections Work or Code Enforcement Functions.

attachments.name: SMLU24-093 Staff Report Blue Lake Cove Future Land Use

description:
The applicant is requesting the future land use designation be amended for a ±15.50-acre parcel located on the northwest corner of S. Blue Lake Ave. & E. Beresford Ave. from Volusia County’s Urban Low-Intensity (VC: ULI) land use designation to the City of DeLand’s Low-Density Residential (LDR) land use designation.
On December 11, 2024, the Planning Board voted 6-1 to recommend approval of the land use amendment request.
On January 22, 2025, the City Commission voted 3-1 to approve the land use amendment request, on first reading.
On February 18, 2025, ​Volusia County Growth Management Commission (VGMC) sent a letter of no objection.
At first reading, discussion ensued regarding the appropriateness of the Low Density Residential (LDR) land use designation versus the Transitional Residential Development (TRD) designation.
The TRD land use designation is intended for areas on the outskirts of the City to act as a transitional land use between larger-lot development or existing agricultural uses, and lower-density development. The allotted density within the TRD designation is up to 2 dwelling units per acre. The density may be increased up to as much as 3.25 dwelling units per acre if certain performance-based criteria are met, such as enhanced amenities and cluster-development.
In this case, the subject property is located in an area that is predominately residential, with multiple residential subdivisions nearby and well within the City's Urban Core. The current County land use designation of the subject property is Urban Low Intensity (ULI), allowing for density up to 4 dwelling units per acre. The proposed LDR designation with an allotted density of 5.8 units per acre is most appropriate and is compatible and in harmony with the surrounding area. Alternatively, the TRD land use designation would reduce the density entitlements that already exist on the property and would not be in line with development in the immediate area. It is the opinion of staff that the land use change to LDR is the most appropriate land use designation for the subject property, as it will fit in best with the surrounding area, while still maintaining the existing entitlements.
title: Second Reading of Ordinance No. 2025-02, Changing the Land Use for Approximately ±15.50 Acres of Property, Located at the Northwest Corner of South Blue Lake Avenue and East Beresford Avenue, from Volusia County Urban Low Intensity (ULI) to City of DeLand Low Density Residential (LDR).

description:

The Model Administrative Code, Chapter 1 for the Eight Edition (2023) Florida Building Code was used as the format for the updated language. Enforcement standards and procedures were also updated.
There is also a companion RCA related to Chapters 9, 10 and 25.

description:
The provisions of Chapter 9 which were adopted in 1991 are obsolete. In November 2007, the City entered into an interlocal agreement with the County to establish a centralized and uniform system for local registration and discipline of registered contractors, a listing and discipline of state certified contractors pursuant to Parts I and II, Chapter 489, Florida Statutes and the regulation and discipline of local specialty contractors pursuant to Chapter 33 Volusia County Code of Ordinances.
The provisions of Chapter 25, which were adopted in 1991 and subject to multiple amendments, are obsolete. The State of Florida has not used this code since 2001 and all current plumbing code references are contained in the 2023 Florida Plumbing Code.
The provisions of Chapter 10 which were adopted in 2000 have not been amended to reflect subsequent national code changes. The proposed amendments reflect these changes so that it is up-to-date with the current National Electric Code. description:
Tehrani Consulting Engineering has requested permission to remove one historic tree located at 1455 N McDonald Avenue. The Land Development Regulations require that, before the removal of any historic trees should occur, it must be approved by the City Commission. Section 33-57.05(d) states that there must be a finding that the tree is a hazard (due to health or natural damage) or that it is not economically or practically feasible to develop the parcel without removing the tree.
The City Forester has determined that the tree proposed for removal is a 31” DBH historic Red Cedar in fair condition. The applicant requested the removal because construction of the project cannot be accomplished without removing the tree.
At their February 11, 2025 meeting, the Tree Advisory Committee recommended APPROVAL of the removal of the 31” DBH Red Cedar tree because the applicant had demonstrated that construction of the project could not be accomplished without removing the tree.
The Tree Advisory Committee recommended that one hundred percent DBH replacement be required for the historic tree approved for removal. The minimum size for replacement trees is six inch caliper and seventeen feet height.
title: Resolution Approving the Removal of One Historic Tree Located at 1455 North McDonald Avenue.

description: A class action lawsuit is currently pending against various manufacturers of Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) chemicals. There are settlements that have been entered into on behalf of all public water systems and the City of DeLand is automatically a member of the class and entitled to proceeds from the settlements. In order to partake in the settlement distribution, a significant amount of data needs to be provided to the court by each supplier seeking a distribution of settlement proceeds. It will be impractical to have City staff undertake this effort and, more importantly, there are a number of procedural pitfalls that could jeopardize obtaining the full amount of the settlement proceeds. As such, City staff, based upon the advice of the City Attorney, recommends hiring a law firm to handle this for the City. Additionally, in the event that there are future PFAS-related settlements, it is recommended that the City Manager, acting with the advice and consent of the City Attorney, be authorized to execute documents necessary to effectuate recovery of the settlement funds and to authorize the retained law firm to attempt to collect monies for the City in other cases that have not yet been settled.
title: Consideration re Retention of Law Firm for PFAS Class Action Litigation.

description:
In the 23/24 fiscal budget, the City Commission approved a new capital project to design improvements to the Biosolids Dewatering Facility at the Wiley M. Nash Water Reclamation Facility. This was based on receiving an additional $15,000,000 million dollar Water Quality Improvement (WQI) grant from the state. This project will replace and increase the capacity of the thirty-five-year-old biosolids handling building and its associated equipment.
The design task order was awarded to Mead & Hunt in February 2024. Their task assignment did not include any approval for additional funds for construction engineering and inspection (CEI) services in the task order that was approved by the City Commission. It was noted that once design and bidding was complete a new task assignment would be provided at a future meeting for approval.
Thus, after a year of design, permitting, grant and loan applications, and multiple meetings by the design team of engineers, city staff, and the CMAR team, we have reached the point of pending construction to commence. To ensure that all of the construction will be following permitting, grants, and loan documents over next 18 months, it is staff’s opinion that a company should be hired to do so on behalf of the city.
An agreement is in place between the City and Mead & Hunt per RFQ #22-01 that places this scope of work in their proposal. The subject task order, if approved, will provide services for the project management, construction engineering and inspection (CEI) services, construction observation, project closeout, funding assistance, subconsultants and reimbursables, and a contingency allowance under city control for the 18 months of proposed construction duration by the CMAR contractor.
title: Consideration re Task Order Assignment, Wiley M. Nash WRF Dewatering Improvements CEI and EOR Services.

description: At their February 5, 2024 meeting, the City Commission awarded a FDOT grant in the amount of $16,000 to design T-hangar Electrical Improvements project. It consisted of replacing the existing electrical services at T-hangars A, B, C, and upgrading the electrical equipment in each T-hangar unit. The original grant has been amended to include construction costs. It is anticipated that the current meters, disconnects, and panels will be replaced and upsized. The project will also include exterior wall pack lighting upgrades, and a photocell and timer-controlled contactors for lighting the T-hangar taxilanes in between the buildings. Pursuant to applications made by staff and our consultant, Avcon, the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) has agreed to fund 80% ($140,000.00) of the total construction cost of $175,000.00.

attachments.name: Edgewood - Utility Eeasement to City Deland (Executed)

description:
TLC Edgewater, LLC will be constructing a subdivision at the SW intersection of Beresford Road and Fatio Road in Volusia County. As a condition of approval for the proposed subdivision, the City Utilities Department requested that a dedicated area be set aside for the River Booster Pump Station project. The developer has it shown on the subdivision preliminary plat as BP-1 tract dedicated to the City of DeLand.
The River Booster Pump Station project was awarded to McMahan in October of 2024, however, due to an unresolved conflict concerning the development order with Volusia County, the project continues to be delayed. Staff has been unable to secure a building permit thus far and has been working with both parties to kick off construction. The City has a large St. John’s River Water Management District (SJRWMD) grant that is tied to this project, and we are quickly approaching the deadline for project completion.
Staff has evaluated several options to get the project moving: The developer is placing our project into phase #1 per county, to separate from the rest of the development to give us a development order. Meanwhile the rest of the subdivision will be considered phase #2. In addition, the developer has agreed to grant the City an easement over the proposed tract, and access off of Beresford Rd. to construct the River Booster Pump Station.
The City Attorney has assisted in this endeavor by drafting an easement agreement between the City and the Developer. The Developer has reviewed the agreement, and signed it. Once the easement has been accepted by the City and recorded, we can provide it to Volusia County and McMahan should be able to finalize and obtain the building permit from Volusia County.
title: Consideration re Acceptance of Utility Easement from TLC Edgewater, LLC for the River Booster Pump Station Site Located at 1626 West Beresford Avenue.
